blocks.text: Or rather, that, having taken wings from that daughter of hers, she spent her last years in lofty towers? [II, 529] Lucian in De Syria Dea: Τὸ Σεμιράμιος τέλος εἰς περιστερὰν ἀπίκετο [To Semiramios telos eis peristeran apiketo], Semiramis was at last turned into a dove. Athenagoras, in the Legatio, on the same woman: Τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον, εἰς περιστερὰν μετέβαλεν ἡ γυνή· ὁ μύθος παρὰ Κτησίᾳ [To gar adynaton, eis peristeran metebalen hē gynē; ho mythos para Ktēsia]. For, what is impossible, the woman was changed into a dove. The tale is found in Ctesias. This is why among the Syrians and Assyrians doves were held in great veneration, as Ctesias teaches in Diodorus, after relating that Semiramis was nourished by doves and also took her name from them: Ἃς ἀπ᾽ ἐκείνων τῶν χρόνων, οἱ κατὰ Συρίαν ἅπαντες διετέλεσαν, ὡς Θεὰς τιμῶντες [Has ap᾽ ekeinōn tōn chronōn, hoi kata Syrian hapantes dietelesan, hōs Theas timōntes]; These, from those times on, all the Syrians have never ceased to worship as goddesses. And after the story of her metamorphosis into a dove the same author adds: Διὸ καὶ τοὺς Ἀσσυρίους τὴν περιστερὰν τιμᾷν ὡς Θεὸν, ἀπαθανατίζοντες τὴν Σεμίραμιν [Dio kai tous Assyrious tēn peristeran timan hōs Theon, apathanatizontes tēn Semiramin]; Hence the Assyrians also venerate the dove as a goddess, in order to rescue Semiramis from death. Xenophon too, in book 1 of the Cyrus the Younger, speaking of the fish of the Chalus, a river of Syria: Οὓς οἱ Σύροι Θεοὺς ἐνόμιζον, καὶ ἀδικεῖν οὐκ εἴων, οὐδὲ τὰς περιστεράς [Hous hoi Syroi Theous enomizon, kai adikein ouk eiōn, oude tas peristeras]. These the Syrians regarded as gods, and forbade anyone to harm them, as also the doves. Philo in Eusebius, near the end of book 8 of the Praeparatio Evangelica: Ἀμήχανόν τι πελειάδων πλῆθος ἐπὶ τῶν τριόδων, καὶ κατ᾽ οἰκίαν ἑκάστην, ἐθεασάμην. πυνθανομένῳ δέ μοι τὴν αἰτίαν ἔφασαν, οὐ θεμιτὸν εἶναι συλλαμβάνειν. ἀπειρῆσθαι γὰρ ἐκ παλαίου τοῖς οἰκήτορσι τὴν χρῆσιν [Amēchanon ti peleiadōn plēthos epi tōn triodōn, kai kat᾽ oikian hekastēn, etheasamēn. pynthanomenō de moi tēn aitian ephasan, ou themiton einai syllambanein. apeirēsthai gar ek palaiou tois oikētorsi tēn chrēsin]. I saw an immense multitude of doves at the crossroads and in every house (at Ascalon). And when I asked the reason, they answered that it was unlawful to catch them, for their use had long ago been forbidden to the inhabitants. Tibullus, Elegy 8:
The white dove, sacred to the man of Palestine.
